name: Cat's Claw
summary: Inner-bark vine containing pentacyclic oxindole alkaloids that modulate immunity and inhibit NF-kB. A 2002 randomized controlled trial (Journal of Rheumatology) showed reduced pain and swelling in rheumatoid arthritis; NCCIH acknowledges anti-inflammatory action but calls evidence insufficient for most claims.
how: Bark tea: simmer 1-2 g dried bark 15 minutes, 1-3 cups daily. Standardized capsules 250-350 mg, 1-3 times daily. Tincture also available.
safety: Avoid with immunosuppressant drugs - it may counteract them - and with HIV protease inhibitors. May lower blood pressure. Anticoagulant properties: stop before surgery. Contraindicated in pregnancy. Verify the species is U. tomentosa, not U. guianensis.
origin: Ashaninka healers boiled the thorned vine's bark for deep body cleansing, joint inflammation and ulcers.

name: Maca Root
summary: High-altitude Andean root with multiple clinical trials supporting improved sexual desire and libido, small-trial improvements in sperm quality, and some benefit for menopausal hot flashes and mood. Notably it does not appear to alter testosterone or estrogen levels directly.
how: Gelatinized powder 1.5-3 g daily in smoothies, coffee or food; capsules 500-1000 mg, 2-3 times daily. Three varieties: yellow (general), red (prostate, bone density), black (sperm, memory). Start low and build up; raw maca is hard to digest.
safety: Generally well tolerated. Contains goitrogens - caution with thyroid conditions (cooking/gelatinization reduces them). May cause initial digestive upset. Avoid in hormone-sensitive conditions pending more research.
origin: Cultivated above 3,800 m for 2,000+ years; Incan warriors reportedly ate maca before battle for stamina.

name: Quinoa
summary: A complete protein containing all nine essential amino acids, high in fiber, magnesium, iron and B vitamins with a low glycemic index. Studies show cardiovascular benefits including reduced cholesterol and triglycerides; naturally gluten-free and rich in quercetin and kaempferol.
how: Rinse well to remove the bitter saponin coat, then simmer 1:2 quinoa to water for 15-20 minutes. Use as a rice substitute, in salads, soups and breakfast bowls. White, red and black varieties are all nutritious.
safety: Unrinsed saponins can irritate the gut. High oxalate content - caution with a history of kidney stones. Rare allergic reactions reported.
origin: The sacred "mother grain" of the Inca empire, planted each season by the emperor with a golden spade.

name: Cacao
aka: Theobroma cacao, raw chocolate, cocoa flavanols
summary: Flavanol-rich bean; the large COSMOS trial showed cocoa flavanol supplementation improved cardiovascular outcomes, and meta-analyses confirm blood pressure reduction and improved endothelial function. Theobromine is a mild bronchodilator, and mood effects link to serotonin precursors and endorphin release.
how: Raw cacao powder 1-2 tbsp daily in smoothies or hot drinks; cacao nibs as a snack; dark chocolate at 70%+ cacao; ceremonial-grade minimally processed cacao. Avoid Dutch-processed/alkalized cocoa, which destroys flavanols.
safety: Caffeine and theobromine can cause insomnia, anxiety or rapid heartbeat in sensitive people, and may trigger migraines. Can interact with MAOIs. Contains oxalates. Some sources are high in cadmium - choose tested brands. Toxic to dogs and cats.
origin: "Food of the Gods" - Mayan xocolatl and Aztec ceremonial drink; cacao beans served as Aztec currency.

name: Yerba Mate
summary: Contains caffeine, theobromine and theophylline for a balanced stimulant effect, plus saponins and polyphenols with antioxidant capacity rivaling green tea. Studies show thermogenic fat-oxidation effects supporting weight management and improved lipid profiles in clinical trials.
how: Traditional: loose leaf in a gourd with a bombilla, using hot but not boiling water (~70-80C). Also as tea bags, cold-brewed terere, or in energy drinks. 1-3 cups daily is typical.
safety: Habitual consumption of very hot mate is classified IARC Group 2A "probably carcinogenic" and linked to esophageal cancer - the risk is attributed to temperature, so drink it warm, not scalding. Contains caffeine; may interact with stimulant medications, MAOIs, adenosine and lithium.
origin: Drunk by the Guarani long before European contact and shared communally from a gourd; the "drink of the gods".

name: Pau d'Arco
summary: Inner bark containing lapachol and beta-lapachone with strong antifungal, antibacterial and antiparasitic activity in lab studies, including well-documented anti-Candida effects. Beta-lapachone shows antitumor activity in vitro and in animals as complementary interest only; lapachol was dropped by the NCI due to toxicity, and human trials are lacking.
how: Decoction: simmer 1 tbsp dried inner bark in 2 cups water 15-20 minutes; 1-3 cups daily for limited 2-3 week periods. Capsules 500-1000 mg, 2-3 times daily. Tincture available.
safety: High doses cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Lapachol thins the blood - avoid with anticoagulants and before surgery. Do not use in pregnancy (possibly embryotoxic). May interact with chemotherapy drugs. Not for long-term continuous use; product quality varies enormously.
origin: Amazonian, Incan and Calawaya healers boiled the bark as a fever remedy and "blood purifier".

name: Acai Berry
summary: Amazonian palm berry with extremely high anthocyanin content (cyanidin-3-glucoside) and among the highest ORAC scores of any fruit. Clinical studies show improved lipid profiles and vascular function, and a 2011 pilot trial found reduced metabolic disease markers; cancer effects are in vitro only.
how: Unsweetened frozen puree blended into bowls or smoothies; freeze-dried powder 1-2 tsp daily; juice (watch added sugar); supplements 500-1000 mg daily. Must be processed or frozen quickly after harvest since it degrades rapidly.
safety: Highly perishable and most commercial products are heavily processed or contain little real acai. Calorie-dense in traditional quantities. Manganese content may affect MRI results. Rare allergy in those sensitive to palm pollen. Beware multi-level marketing scams.
origin: A staple of Amazonian riverine communities, pulped into a thick purple paste eaten with fish and cassava.

name: Graviola / Soursop
summary: Acetogenins such as annonacin are cytotoxic to cancer cell lines in vitro, but no human cancer trials exist and Memorial Sloan Kettering advises against its use; it is not a cancer treatment and at most a controversial complementary-support claim. Antiparasitic, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects are confirmed.
how: Fruit eaten fresh or in smoothies with seeds removed. Leaf tea: 1-2 g dried leaves steeped 5-10 minutes, occasional use only. Capsules and extracts available.
safety: SERIOUS: chronic consumption may cause neurodegeneration (atypical Parkinsonism) from annonacin - a documented risk in Caribbean populations; avoid long-term daily leaf tea. Seeds are toxic - never consume. Do NOT substitute for cancer treatment. May lower blood pressure excessively; avoid with antihypertensive and antidiabetic medications. Contraindicated in pregnancy.
origin: Used across Amazonian, Central American and Caribbean traditions for parasites, fever and as a sedative.

name: Sangre de Grado
summary: Red tree latex whose active proanthocyanidin, crofelemer, became the FDA-approved drug Fulyzaq/Mytesi (2012) for HIV/AIDS-associated diarrhea - one of the few approved drugs derived directly from a traditional botanical. Taspine and proanthocyanidins give documented wound-healing acceleration and antimicrobial activity.
how: Topical: apply raw latex directly to cuts, scrapes and bites, where it forms a fast-drying "second skin" (stings briefly). Internal: 3-5 drops in water, 1-3 times daily, short-term. Prescription Mytesi/Fulyzaq for diarrhea.
safety: Internal use may cause nausea and is not well studied long-term. Contraindicated in pregnancy due to taspine. Ensure correct species - several trees yield red sap. Sustainable, authentic sourcing is a concern.
origin: One of the most important wound remedies in Amazonian medicine across Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.

name: Chuchuhuasi
summary: Bark tonic containing phenoldienone triterpenes, proanthocyanidins and maytansine alkaloids, with anti-inflammatory and muscle-relaxant effects documented in animal studies. Maytansine derivatives underpin modern antibody-drug conjugates such as Kadcyla, though the raw bark itself has no human trials.
how: Traditional bark tincture macerated in cane alcohol (aguardiente); bark decoction or tea; capsules from specialist suppliers. Typically taken in 2-4 week courses.
safety: Limited human safety data. Avoid during pregnancy. May potentiate muscle relaxants and sedatives. Not recommended for long-term continuous use. Confirm correct species identification.
origin: Quechua for "trembling back" - drunk as a tincture for joint and back pain and as an aphrodisiac tonic.

name: Muna
summary: Andean mint whose essential oil (pulegone, menthone and other terpenes) has documented antibacterial and antifungal activity, plus in vitro antiparasitic effects against Giardia. Traditionally the go-to tea for stomach upset and altitude sickness (soroche).
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp fresh or dried leaves in hot water 5-10 minutes. Widely sold in Andean markets and used as a culinary seasoning; leaves rubbed on the body for headache.
safety: Contains pulegone, which is hepatotoxic in quantity (as in pennyroyal). Do NOT use the essential oil internally and avoid concentrated extracts - stick to whole-leaf tea in moderation. Avoid during pregnancy.
origin: An Andean kitchen and altitude remedy across Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador; also used as an insect repellent.

name: Sacha Inchi
summary: One of the richest plant sources of omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid (~47%) with ~27% complete protein and high vitamin E. Clinical studies show improved lipid profiles - lower LDL, higher HDL - and its omega-3 to omega-6 ratio is superior to most plant oils.
how: Roasted seeds as a snack; cold-pressed oil 1-2 tbsp daily, never heated (heat destroys the omega-3s); protein powder from the pressed seed cake; oil applied to skin.
safety: Raw seeds contain alkaloids and must be roasted or cooked before eating. The oil is highly perishable - store refrigerated in a dark bottle. Nut-like allergic reactions possible.
origin: Cultivated in Peru for 3,000+ years and depicted in Moche pottery; seeds roasted as food, oil used on skin.

name: Lucuma
aka: Pouteria lucuma, Gold of the Incas
summary: A low-glycemic natural sweetener containing beta-carotene, iron, zinc, niacin and polyphenols. In vitro studies show alpha-glucosidase inhibition suggesting blood sugar regulation potential, and wound-healing properties are documented in animal studies.
how: Freeze-dried powder 1-2 tbsp used as a natural sweetener in smoothies, desserts and baking; it has a subtle maple-caramel flavor and is sold in health food stores.
safety: Generally very safe. Rare allergic reactions. It is caloric, not a calorie-free sweetener. Limited safety data for concentrated supplements.
origin: A symbol of fertility and creation in Incan mythology, eaten fresh and dried and applied to wounds.

name: Camu Camu
summary: Amazonian riverbank fruit containing 2-3% vitamin C by weight - 30-60 times more than oranges per serving - plus ellagic acid and anthocyanins. A 2018 study in Gut showed camu camu altered gut microbiota, prevented obesity and improved metabolic markers in mice; anti-inflammatory effects exceed equivalent synthetic vitamin C.
how: Freeze-dried powder 1/2 to 1 tsp daily in smoothies, juice or water; capsules 500-1000 mg daily. Very sour, so mix with other flavors; the whole-food form is preferred over isolated vitamin C.
safety: High vitamin C can cause digestive upset at high doses and increases iron absorption - caution in hemochromatosis. May interact with chemotherapy drugs and can interfere with certain lab tests. Very sour - dilute to protect tooth enamel.
origin: Harvested from Amazonian floodplains and eaten or drunk as a cold and infection tonic.

name: Annatto
summary: Seed carotenoids bixin and norbixin are strong antioxidants with documented antimicrobial and UV-protective properties, and the seeds' tocotrienols showed lipid-lowering effects in clinical trials. Some evidence supports blood sugar regulation; widely used as natural colorant E160b.
how: Achiote paste in Latin American cooking; seeds steeped in oil for cooking; tocotrienol supplements; traditional topical preparations for skin conditions and burns.
safety: Allergic reactions are rare but documented, including urticaria, and some people react to annatto as a food additive. May affect blood sugar - monitor if diabetic. Stains skin and clothing intensely.
origin: Used across tropical America as ceremonial body paint, sun protection, insect repellent and food coloring.

name: Guayusa
summary: Amazonian holly leaf with caffeine at roughly 3% of dry weight plus L-theanine, theobromine and chlorogenic acids. The caffeine-plus-L-theanine combination is well studied for calm alertness, and its polyphenol and antioxidant content is comparable to coffee.
how: Steep 1-2 tsp dried leaf in hot water for 4-7 minutes; also sold as tea bags, loose leaf and in energy drinks, and can be cold-brewed. Less bitter than yerba mate.
safety: Contains caffeine - the same precautions as other caffeinated drinks apply, and it may interfere with sleep if taken late. Less studied than yerba mate or green tea.
origin: Kichwa communities brew it communally before dawn as a "night watchman's" tea for alertness and lucid dreaming.

name: Coca Leaf
summary: The whole leaf is pharmacologically distinct from cocaine: 0.5-1% cocaine alkaloid among 14+ alkaloids, giving a mild coffee-like effect with slow, limited absorption. WHO/UNICEF studies (1995) found traditional use is not linked to addiction, and it relieves altitude sickness symptoms.
how: Leaves chewed with an alkaline llipta (lime or ash), or brewed as mate de coca. Legal as leaf/tea in Bolivia, Peru and parts of Colombia and Argentina.
safety: LEGAL WARNING: coca leaf is illegal in most countries outside the Andes and possession can bring serious criminal penalties; it may also produce a positive drug test. Contraindicated in heart conditions. Overuse causes insomnia and stomach upset. Do not confuse traditional leaf use with cocaine.
origin: A sacred Andean plant for 8,000+ years, offered to Pachamama and chewed by miners, farmers and travelers.

name: Passionflower
summary: Approved by the European Medicines Agency for mild stress and sleep disorders. A randomized trial (Akhondzadeh 2001) found it comparable to the benzodiazepine oxazepam for generalized anxiety with fewer side effects, and a 2020 systematic review confirmed anxiolytic effects via GABA-A modulation.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp dried herb 10-15 minutes, 1-3 cups daily. Tincture 1-2 mL three times daily. Capsules 400-800 mg standardized extract. Often combined with valerian and lemon balm for sleep.
safety: Enhances the effects of sedatives, benzodiazepines and alcohol. Do not use with MAOIs (contains small amounts of harmala alkaloids). Avoid in pregnancy - may stimulate uterine contractions. Causes drowsiness: caution when driving.
origin: Used by the Aztecs as a sedative and analgesic; named for the Passion of Christ by European colonizers.

name: Damiana
summary: Traditional aphrodisiac and nerve tonic containing apigenin (a mild anxiolytic), terpenes and arbutin. Animal studies support anxiolytic and pro-sexual effects and one small human study found improved sexual satisfaction in a combination formula, but clinical validation is weak.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tsp dried leaves 10-15 minutes. Tincture 2-4 mL, 2-3 times daily. Capsules available; traditional Mexican damiana liqueur persists as an aphrodisiac.
safety: May affect blood sugar and interact with diabetes medications. Potential estrogenic effects - avoid in hormone-sensitive cancers. High doses may rarely cause hallucinations. Avoid during pregnancy.
origin: A Mayan and Aztec tonic for nervousness and low libido; the Mayan name translates as "plant for asthma".

name: Copaiba Oil
summary: Tree oleoresin exceptionally high in beta-caryophyllene, a selective CB2 cannabinoid receptor agonist that produces anti-inflammatory effects without psychoactivity - one of the best-documented mechanisms in botanical medicine. Anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, analgesic and wound-healing effects confirmed in animal and some human studies.
how: Topical: dilute roughly 1:3 in carrier oil for skin. Internal: 1-3 drops in a capsule or honey, short-term. Ensure true copaiba oleoresin rather than a steam-distilled version, which has a different profile.
safety: May irritate sensitive skin - patch test first. Internal use is controversial among practitioners. May interact with blood-thinning medications. Frequently adulterated - verify purity. Avoid during pregnancy.
origin: Tapped directly from Amazonian tree trunks and applied to wounds or taken in drops for sore throat and cystitis.

name: Andiroba Oil
summary: Seed oil containing limonoids (andirobin, gedunin) with documented anti-inflammatory, antimalarial and insect-repellent properties. Gedunin's anti-inflammatory activity is comparable to some NSAIDs in animal models, and repellency against Aedes aegypti mosquitoes is confirmed.
how: Apply topically to skin, insect bites and inflamed joints, or use as a massage oil, often blended with other oils. Available from Brazilian natural product suppliers; traditionally burned in candles as a repellent.
safety: Primarily for external use - internal use is not well studied. May cause allergic skin reactions. Frequently adulterated with cheaper oils, so verify sourcing.
origin: Amazonian communities pressed the seeds for swollen joints, bruises, rashes and mosquito protection.

name: Brazil Nut
summary: The richest food source of selenium on Earth - one nut supplies 70-90 mcg, exceeding the RDA - which is essential for thyroid T4-to-T3 conversion and glutathione peroxidase. Clinical trials show 1-2 nuts daily normalize selenium status and improve cholesterol (higher HDL, lower LDL).
how: Eat 1-3 nuts daily and no more - this is a remedy where more is definitively not better. Raw or lightly roasted; store in the refrigerator or freezer because of the high fat content.
safety: DO NOT overconsume: selenium toxicity (selenosis) causes hair loss, brittle nails, nausea and neurological problems. Limit to 1-3 nuts daily. High in barium and calories; may harbor aflatoxins if stored badly. Tree nut allergy applies. Slightly elevated natural radium is negligible at normal intake.
origin: A major Amazonian food and trade item from sacred trees that cannot be farmed without intact forest.

name: Boldo Leaf
summary: Contains boldine, one of the most potent natural antioxidants, with documented anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties and a confirmed choleretic (bile-stimulating) effect. Approved by German Commission E for dyspeptic complaints and mild GI spasms.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 g dried leaves 10 minutes, 1-2 cups daily, preferably before meals. Tincture available; often combined with milk thistle for liver support.
safety: Contains ascaridole, a toxic peroxide - do NOT use the essential oil internally, and excessive doses are toxic. Avoid in bile duct obstruction and severe liver disease. Contraindicated in pregnancy. Anticoagulant effect - may interact with blood thinners. Do not use long-term continuously.
origin: Mapuche machi healers have brewed boldo for liver and gallbladder complaints for thousands of years.

name: Quillay (Soapbark)
summary: Quillaja saponins (QS-21) are a critical component of modern vaccine adjuvants used in Shingrix, Mosquirix and the Novavax COVID-19 vaccine, dramatically enhancing both humoral and cell-mediated immunity. Traditional expectorant and antimicrobial properties are confirmed.
how: Primarily external: bark shavings in water as a natural foaming shampoo or cleanser. Very dilute bark tea for coughs. Commercially used as a foaming agent in foods, beverages (root beer) and cosmetics.
safety: Saponins are hemolytic - toxic to red blood cells if injected, and they should not be applied to open wounds. Concentrated internal use causes GI irritation, nausea and diarrhea; use only mild preparations internally (saponins are poorly absorbed orally in small amounts).
origin: Mapuche used the saponin-rich inner bark as soap, shampoo, wound wash and cough expectorant.

name: Moringa
aka: Moringa oleifera, Tree of Life, ben oil
summary: Exceptionally nutrient-dense dried leaf with isothiocyanates showing anti-inflammatory and blood-sugar-lowering effects in clinical trials; a 2019 systematic review found evidence for glucose reduction. Antihypertensive effects are shown in animal studies, and crushed seeds are well-documented water purifiers via flocculation proteins.
how: Dried leaf powder 1-2 tsp daily in food or smoothies; fresh leaves cooked as greens; capsules 500-1000 mg, 1-2 times daily; moringa tea; ben oil for skin and hair.
safety: Avoid the root and root bark - they contain the potentially toxic alkaloid spirochin. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure - monitor if on medications. May interfere with thyroid medication (levothyroxine). Avoid in pregnancy (root bark can cause uterine contractions; leaf evidence is limited). Start with small doses.
origin: Adopted enthusiastically into Caribbean and African bush medicine, with every part of the tree used.

name: Turmeric
summary: Curcumin is among the most researched natural compounds, inhibiting NF-kB, COX-2 and LOX. Clinical trials show efficacy in osteoarthritis (comparable to ibuprofen in some studies), depression as an SSRI adjunct, metabolic syndrome and inflammatory bowel conditions. Poor bioavailability is the key limitation.
how: Powder 1-3 g daily taken with fat and black pepper (piperine raises absorption ~2000%); curcumin supplements 500-1000 mg standardized extract with piperine. Fresh root grated into golden milk or Caribbean turmeric punch with rum, lime and honey; paste applied to sprains.
safety: Antiplatelet effect - may interact with blood thinners; stop high-dose supplements before surgery. May worsen gallbladder disease and interfere with iron absorption. Long-term high-dose curcumin supplements carry rare reports of liver injury. Stains everything yellow.
origin: Brought by East Indian indentured labourers and absorbed into Afro-Caribbean bush medicine.

name: Ginger Beer
summary: Multiple meta-analyses confirm ginger's efficacy for nausea - pregnancy-related, chemotherapy-induced and postoperative. Gingerols and shogaols inhibit COX-2 and 5-LOX, reduce post-exercise muscle pain, and clinical trials show blood sugar lowering.
how: Homemade ginger beer: blend fresh ginger root, strain, add lime, sweetener and water (fermented or not) - far stronger than commercial ginger ale. Fresh ginger tea: steep a 1-inch sliced root 10 minutes. Capsules 250-500 mg up to four times daily.
safety: Mild anticoagulant - may interact with blood thinners. Causes heartburn or GI irritation at high doses. May lower blood sugar - monitor with diabetes medications. Fermented versions contain small amounts of alcohol; excess irritates the mouth and throat.
origin: A Jamaican, Trinidadian and Barbadian household remedy for nausea, colds and as a warming tonic.

name: Noni (Caribbean Bush Medicine)
aka: Morinda citrifolia, vomit fruit, cheese fruit
summary: Introduced from the Pacific and absorbed into Caribbean bush medicine, where the notoriously foul-smelling juice is drunk as a general health tonic and the leaves are used as a pain poultice. Evidence mirrors the Polynesian noni entry: moderate, based on iridoids, scopoletin and analgesic trial data.
how: Juice 1-2 oz daily, usually mixed with other juices to mask the taste. Leaves applied as a poultice for pain and inflammation; ripe fruit applied to skin infections and wounds.
safety: High in potassium - caution with kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics. Contains vitamin K and may interfere with warfarin. Rare hepatotoxicity case reports. May interact with ACE inhibitors. Many commercial products are heavily diluted.
origin: Carried from the Pacific Islands into Caribbean yards and adopted as a general-purpose bush remedy.

name: Cerasee / Bitter Melon
summary: Contains charantin, polypeptide-p (plant insulin) and vicine with documented hypoglycemic activity through three mechanisms: increased insulin secretion, better glucose uptake and inhibited glucose absorption. Multiple clinical trials show blood-sugar lowering in type 2 diabetes, though meta-analyses are inconsistent.
how: Tea: boil leaves and vine 10-15 minutes, drink 1/2 to 1 cup (extremely bitter). Fruit cooked and eaten. Capsules 500-1000 mg, 1-3 times daily; diluted juice. Traditional Caribbean use is intermittent - a 9-day course, not continuous.
safety: Can cause dangerous hypoglycemia combined with diabetes medications - monitor blood sugar closely. Vicine can trigger favism in G6PD deficiency. Avoid in pregnancy - documented abortifacient properties. Causes diarrhea and abdominal pain. Seeds and the red arils around them are toxic, especially to children.
origin: Jamaica's most important "washout" bush tea, drunk for nine days as a spring cleaning tonic.

name: Fever Grass / Lemongrass
summary: Rich in citral, geraniol and myrcene with documented antibacterial, antifungal and anti-inflammatory properties. Anxiolytic effects appear in animal studies and a small human trial; analgesic, antipyretic and mosquito-repellent activity are documented.
how: Tea: bruise 2-3 fresh stalks and steep 10 minutes - pleasantly lemony. Used in soups and curries. Essential oil for aromatherapy; diluted topical oil for muscle pain; baths for muscle relaxation.
safety: Very safe as tea. The essential oil should never be taken internally in concentrated form and can cause contact dermatitis; avoid essential oil use in pregnancy. May lower blood sugar slightly and may interact with sedatives.
origin: Grown in nearly every Caribbean yard and boiled for fevers - hence "fever grass".

name: Sorrel / Hibiscus
summary: Meta-analyses confirm significant blood pressure reduction: a 2015 Journal of Hypertension analysis found -7.6 mmHg systolic and -3.5 mmHg diastolic, and one head-to-head trial found it comparable to captopril. It also lowers LDL cholesterol and has strong anthocyanin antioxidant activity and a mild diuretic effect.
how: Tea: steep 1-2 tbsp dried calyces 15-20 minutes (or cold brew); 2-3 cups daily for blood pressure. Caribbean sorrel drink: boil calyces with ginger, cloves and cinnamon. Widely sold as hibiscus tea bags.
safety: May drop blood pressure too far alongside antihypertensive medications. Mildly estrogenic - caution in hormone-sensitive conditions. Interferes with acetaminophen metabolism, reduces chloroquine absorption, and the diuretic effect may affect lithium levels. Acidic - may worsen reflux.
origin: A beloved Caribbean Christmas drink from West African roselle, drunk year-round for "pressure".

name: Sea Moss / Irish Moss
summary: Mineral-rich seaweed gel high in iodine, potassium, calcium and sulfur, with prebiotic properties and in vitro antiviral activity (carrageenan blocks viral adhesion). The "92 of 102 minerals" claim is marketing - content varies by species and human trials are scarce.
how: Soak dried sea moss 12-24 hours, blend into a gel, add 1-2 tbsp to smoothies, soups or drinks. Traditional drink: blend with nut milk, dates, vanilla and nutmeg. Capsules available.
safety: High iodine can cause thyroid dysfunction if overconsumed - especially risky in Hashimoto's or Graves' disease. Heavy metal contamination is a real risk since seaweed absorbs what is in the water; buy from suppliers who test. Degraded carrageenan (poligeenan) may cause GI inflammation. Start with small amounts.
origin: A Jamaican "male tonic" and chest-cold remedy, blended with condensed milk, nutmeg and vanilla.

name: Guinea Hen Weed
summary: Contains dibenzyl trisulfide and other organosulfur compounds that induce apoptosis in cancer cell lines in vitro with selective cytotoxicity - relevant only as complementary support research, since no human cancer trials exist. Analgesic, anti-inflammatory and immune-stimulating (increased NK cell activity) effects are confirmed in animals.
how: Tea: simmer 1 tbsp dried root or leaves in 2 cups water 10-15 minutes; 1 cup daily for limited periods only. Tincture available.
safety: Contains coumarin with blood-thinning properties - avoid with anticoagulants. May cause uterine contractions: absolutely avoid in pregnancy. May cause hypoglycemia and lower blood sugar. High doses may be toxic. Do not give to children; limited long-term safety data.
origin: A strongly garlic-scented Jamaican bush medicine, also used in Afro-Brazilian Candomble practice.

name: Jack-in-the-Bush
summary: Leaf remedy containing flavonoids (eupolin), alkaloids and tannins, with wound-healing properties confirmed in animal studies through hemostasis and tissue repair. Antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects are documented, but clinical data is absent.
how: Tea: steep fresh or dried leaves 10 minutes for colds, fever and headache. Poultice: crush fresh leaves and apply to minor cuts and wounds to stop bleeding.
safety: May contain hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids - a serious concern; do not use long-term. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Limited safety data. Treated as an invasive weed in many regions and may have been sprayed with herbicide - ensure clean sourcing.
origin: One of the most commonly used "yard remedies" in Jamaica and Trinidad for cuts, colds and fevers.

name: Sarsaparilla
summary: Root containing steroidal saponins (sarsasapogenin, smilagenin), flavonoids and phytosterols. A 1942 New England Journal of Medicine trial showed improvement in psoriasis patients, and endotoxin-binding activity - saponins bind bacterial lipopolysaccharides in the gut - may explain the "blood purifying" reputation.
how: Decoction: simmer 1-2 tsp dried root in 2 cups water 15 minutes, 1-2 cups daily. Tincture 2-4 mL, 2-3 times daily. Capsules available; the classic root beer flavoring.
safety: May cause stomach irritation and has a diuretic effect. Saponins can increase absorption of other drugs and may potentiate digitalis and bismuth. Potential kidney irritation with long-term use. Asthma exacerbation reported in some cases. Steroidal saponins do NOT convert to human testosterone despite marketing claims.
origin: The primary pre-antibiotic treatment for syphilis in the Americas and a classic "blood purifier" and male tonic.

name: Coconut Oil
aka: Cocos nucifera, virgin coconut oil, lauric acid
summary: About 50% lauric acid, which converts to antimicrobial monolaurin in vitro. Clinical evidence supports its use as a moisturizer and skin barrier in atopic dermatitis, and oil pulling reduces Streptococcus mutans in trials. Cardiovascular effects are genuinely controversial - it raises both LDL and HDL.
how: Topical: apply directly to skin and hair. Oil pulling: swish 1 tbsp for 15-20 minutes then spit out. Cooking: suitable for high heat. Choose virgin, cold-pressed, unrefined.
safety: High in saturated fat - the AHA advises against high consumption for heart health, so caution with cardiovascular risk. The MCT marketing is misleading since lauric acid behaves metabolically more like a long-chain fat. Comedogenic on acne-prone facial skin. Calorie-dense. Coconut allergy exists, though tree nut allergy usually does not cross-react.
origin: The "tree of life" across Caribbean and Pacific cultures, used for skin, hair, wounds, cooking and oral health.

name: Aloe Vera
aka: Aloe barbadensis miller, sinkle bible, acemannan
summary: Trials confirm topical gel accelerates burn healing and helps psoriasis and radiation dermatitis, with moderate evidence for oral ulcers. Acemannan is an immunostimulant and wound healer; internal gel shows some evidence for type 2 diabetes and IBS.
how: Topical: fresh gel straight from the cut leaf onto burns, cuts, sunburn and irritations. Internal: clear inner gel only, blended into drinks, or commercial aloe juice.
safety: The yellow latex under the leaf skin is a potent anthraquinone laxative causing severe cramping, diarrhea and electrolyte imbalance; long-term oral latex use is associated with increased colorectal cancer risk (IARC), and the FDA removed oral aloe laxatives from GRAS status in 2002. Use only the clear inner gel internally. Internal use may lower blood sugar and potassium. Rare contact dermatitis.
origin: Called "sinkle bible" in Jamaica and grown in most Caribbean yards as a household cure-all.

name: Kava Kava
summary: Multiple clinical trials and a 2003 Cochrane Review confirm kava is effective for generalized anxiety, with a 2013 RCT showing significant reduction versus placebo. Kavalactones modulate GABA, dopamine and norepinephrine, producing anxiolysis without the cognitive impairment of benzodiazepines.
how: Traditional: ground root kneaded in water and strained. Standardized extracts 60-120 mg kavalactones, 1-3 times daily. Water-based extracts and "noble" varieties are preferred; avoid acetone or ethanol extracts and "tudei" varieties.
safety: Liver toxicity controversy: cases of severe hepatotoxicity and liver failure led to European bans, with risk linked to stem/leaf peelings, solvent extraction, tudei varieties, pre-existing liver disease and combination with alcohol or hepatotoxic drugs. Do NOT combine with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other sedatives. Heavy chronic use causes reversible scaly "kava dermopathy". Avoid in pregnancy.
origin: The most culturally significant Pacific plant for 3,000+ years, central to ceremony, diplomacy and welcome.

name: Tamanu Oil
summary: Nut oil containing calophyllolide, delta-tocotrienol and unique xanthones and coumarins, with wound-healing acceleration shown in clinical studies. Antibacterial against Staphylococcus aureus and the acne bacterium P. acnes; anti-inflammatory effects comparable to indomethacin in animal models, plus fibroblast proliferation and UV protection.
how: Apply undiluted to scars, wounds, blemishes and skin conditions 2-3 times daily, or blend with carrier oils; use as a face oil for acne-prone skin and massage into painful joints. Cold-pressed unrefined oil is best - dark green with a nutty smell.
safety: Tree nut origin, so allergy is possible - patch test before wide use. For external use only. May stain light clothing and has a strong smell. Frequently adulterated - verify sourcing.
origin: A sacred Polynesian healing oil, applied to wounds, burns and even to newborns' skin.

name: Tiare / Monoi Oil
aka: Gardenia taitensis in coconut oil, Monoi de Tahiti
summary: Tahitian gardenia flowers macerated in refined coconut oil. Little studied in its own right - its moisturizing benefits are essentially those of coconut oil plus volatile gardenia compounds that may have mild antimicrobial properties. Tahiti maintains an appellation of origin (AO Monoi de Tahiti) for quality.
how: Apply to skin and hair as a moisturizer, after-sun treatment, hair conditioning treatment or bath oil. Solidifies below ~24C - warm in the hands to liquefy. Look for AO-certified authentic Monoi de Tahiti.
safety: Same cautions as coconut oil: may clog pores on some skin types. Fragrance components can cause sensitization. For external use only.
origin: Tiare flowers steeped for weeks in coconut oil; newborns are anointed with monoi in Tahitian tradition.

name: Taro
summary: A hypoallergenic staple suitable for people with multiple food allergies, containing resistant starch and mucilage with a low glycemic index and rich in fiber, potassium, magnesium and vitamins C and E. Poi shows prebiotic activity promoting Lactobacillus growth; taro polysaccharides show anti-cancer activity in vitro only.
how: The corm must be thoroughly cooked - boiled, steamed, roasted or pounded into poi; leaves must be cooked 40+ minutes. Also eaten as taro chips or baked with taro flour.
safety: NEVER eat raw: raw taro contains calcium oxalate raphides that cause intense burning and swelling of the mouth and throat and can be dangerous. Must be fully cooked. May exacerbate kidney stones (oxalate, reduced by cooking). Handling raw taro irritates skin - wear gloves.
origin: Possibly the oldest cultivated Pacific crop; in Hawaiian mythology Haloa, the taro, is the elder brother of humanity.

name: Kukui Nut Oil
summary: Light nut oil high in linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids, the essential fatty acids that support skin barrier function. Non-comedogenic and fast-absorbing, with preliminary and anecdotal evidence for eczema and psoriasis management; the raw nut's purgative properties are documented.
how: Apply topically to dry skin, eczema patches and after sun exposure; also a good carrier oil for massage. Widely available in Hawaiian skincare products.
safety: Raw nuts are toxic and strongly purgative - only roasted nuts are edible, and the oil is for topical use. Allergic reactions possible. Goes rancid quickly - store refrigerated.
origin: The state tree of Hawaii, burned for light and used by kahuna healers for skin conditions and as a mild laxative.

name: Mamaki Tea
summary: Endemic Hawaiian leaf tea containing catechins, chlorogenic acid and rutin with documented antioxidant activity. Preliminary studies suggest anti-hypertensive and cholesterol-lowering potential; research is limited by the plant's endemic status and small-scale cultivation. Naturally caffeine-free.
how: Steep 1 tbsp dried leaf in hot water 5-10 minutes; mild and pleasant, and can be drunk several times daily. Available from Hawaiian specialty tea companies.
safety: Generally very safe, but with minimal research there is limited safety data. Ensure sustainable and authentic sourcing of this endemic Hawaiian plant.
origin: Brewed by kahuna la'au lapa'au as a general health and fatigue tonic; host plant of the Kamehameha butterfly.

name: Noni Fruit
aka: Morinda citrifolia, nonu, nono, Indian mulberry
summary: Contains iridoids, scopoletin (anti-inflammatory and serotonin-regulating), damnacanthal and polysaccharides. A 2009 clinical trial showed analgesic effects in cervical spondylosis, immune stimulation appears in animal studies, and a University of Hawaii phase I trial found the juice safe at high doses. EFSA approved noni juice as a novel food.
how: Juice 1-2 oz daily, usually mixed with other juices to mask the foul taste; capsules or powder 500-1000 mg, 1-2 times daily; traditional fermented juice; fruit poultice applied to skin conditions.
safety: High in potassium - caution with kidney disease or potassium-sparing diuretics. Contains vitamin K and may interfere with warfarin; may interact with ACE inhibitors. Rare hepatotoxicity reports in Europe, causality debated. Many commercial products are heavily diluted.
origin: A Polynesian "canoe plant" carried by voyagers 2,000+ years ago and one of the most important Pacific medicines.

name: Olena (Hawaiian Turmeric)
summary: The Hawaiian canoe-plant variety of turmeric, sharing curcumin's extensively documented anti-inflammatory profile (NF-kB, COX-2 and LOX inhibition, osteoarthritis trials). Some Hawaiian varieties reportedly carry higher curcumin content, though curcuminoid profiles vary by variety and growing conditions.
how: Grate fresh rhizome into food and drinks as with standard turmeric, taking it with fat and black pepper for absorption. Traditionally the fresh juice was dropped into ears and mixed with salt water as a sinus rinse.
safety: Same as turmeric: antiplatelet effect with blood thinner interaction, stop high doses before surgery, may worsen gallbladder disease and impair iron absorption, rare liver injury with long-term high-dose supplements. Ear drops only under practitioner guidance - dangerous with a perforated eardrum.
origin: Carried to Hawaii as a canoe plant and used for ear and sinus infections, purification rituals and kapa dye.

name: Kawakawa
summary: A kava relative containing myristicin, diayangambin and other lignans with confirmed analgesic effects and compounds related to kavalactones. Diayangambin inhibits cyclooxygenase, and anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity is documented, though clinical trials are lacking.
how: Leaf tea: steep 2-4 fresh or dried leaves 10 minutes. Chew a leaf for toothache (numbing). Leaves used in a poultice for skin conditions, cuts and bruises. Increasingly sold in New Zealand as balms, teas and tinctures.
safety: Contains myristicin, also in nutmeg - high doses can be toxic, causing hallucinations and organ damage; use moderately as a tea. Not recommended in pregnancy. As a kava relative, similar liver concerns may apply with heavy use. Limited formal safety data.
origin: One of the most important plants in Maori rongoa; leaves with insect holes are traditionally held to be more potent.

name: Manuka Honey
aka: Leptospermum scoparium honey, UMF, MGO, Medihoney
summary: Contains methylglyoxal (MGO), graded by the UMF system, and underpins FDA-approved wound products such as Medihoney. Clinically effective against MRSA, MSSA, VRE and other resistant bacteria, with trials supporting diabetic ulcers, burns and surgical wounds plus H. pylori inhibition.
how: Wounds: apply medical-grade manuka (UMF 10+ or MGO 263+) under a dressing. Internal: 1-2 tsp daily for sore throat or digestion. Oral health: dissolve in the mouth. Insist on UMF/MGO certification.
safety: Not for infants under 12 months - botulism risk as with all honey. Diabetics must account for the sugar. Not a substitute for antibiotics in serious infection, and wound application should be monitored by a clinician. Expensive with high rates of fraud - buy certified. Brief stinging on wounds is common; rare allergy.
origin: Maori used manuka bark and leaves long before European honeybees arrived in 1839 made the honey possible.

name: Harakeke / Flax Gel
summary: Mucilaginous leaf-base gel containing polysaccharides and anthraquinones, functionally similar to aloe vera. Preliminary New Zealand university research confirms the traditional wound-healing application, along with documented antimicrobial and antifungal activity; the root contains laxative anthraquinone glycosides.
how: Apply the gel from a cut leaf base directly to burns and wounds, much like aloe vera. Sold in some New Zealand natural health products. Root preparations should be approached with caution.
safety: Root preparations are powerful purgatives - use with extreme caution. Internal use is not well studied. Ensure correct species and preparation; skin sensitivity is possible. Limited availability outside New Zealand.
origin: A cornerstone Maori plant - gel for burns and boils, leaves as bandages, fibers woven into cloth and rope.

name: Koromiko
summary: Leaf decoction containing the iridoid glycosides aucubin and catalpol with documented anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties, plus astringent tannins that support the traditional anti-diarrheal use. Formal clinical research specific to koromiko is very limited.
how: Leaf tea or decoction: boil young leaves 10-15 minutes. Used primarily within New Zealand traditional practice; commercial availability is limited. Leaf poultice for skin ulcers.
safety: Limited safety data and little formal study. Avoid in pregnancy. Best used under the guidance of a rongoa Maori practitioner.
origin: One of the best-known Maori rongoa plants for diarrhea, dysentery and intestinal ulcers.

name: Breadfruit Leaf
summary: Leaf extracts inhibit alpha-glucosidase and alpha-amylase in vitro, suggesting blood sugar regulation, and prenylated flavonoids such as artonin have documented anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity. Hypotensive and ACE-inhibitory effects are shown in animal studies; the fruit itself is a nutritious staple.
how: Leaf tea: simmer 1-2 dried or yellowed leaves in 2 cups water for 15 minutes, drunk for blood sugar management. Fruit cooked as a starchy staple - boiled, roasted or fried.
safety: May lower blood sugar - monitor with diabetes medications - and may lower blood pressure, so caution with antihypertensives. The latex can irritate skin. Human clinical trial data is limited.
origin: A Pacific and Caribbean food staple whose leaf tea is drunk across the Caribbean for "sugar" and "pressure".

name: Tea Tree Oil
summary: One of the best-studied essential oils, with broad-spectrum activity against bacteria (including MRSA in vitro), fungi and some viruses via terpinen-4-ol. Trials confirm efficacy for acne (comparable to 5% benzoyl peroxide), toenail fungus and athlete's foot; TGA-approved topically.
how: Topical only: 5% gel on acne, 10-25% for fungal infections, diluted in carrier oil for wounds, a few drops in shampoo for dandruff. Tea tree toothpaste (do not swallow). Choose ISO 4730 oil.
safety: TOXIC if ingested - even small amounts cause confusion, ataxia and coma; external use only. Can cause contact dermatitis, especially oxidized old oil - store away from light and heat. Estrogenic effects documented, with rare gynecomastia in prepubertal boys from topical use. Not for use in ears. Toxic to cats and dogs. Patch test first.
origin: Bundjalung people crushed the leaves for colds and wounds and bathed in tea tree-steeped lakes.

name: Eucalyptus
summary: 1,8-cineole is a proven expectorant and decongestant approved by German Commission E, with trials showing efficacy in acute bronchitis, sinusitis and COPD and a steroid-sparing adjunct effect in asthma. Antibacterial and antiviral activity documented.
how: Steam inhalation: 3-5 drops in hot water, inhale under a towel. Chest rub diluted 2-3%. Eucalyptol lozenges; cineole capsules 200 mg three times daily for bronchitis (Soledum/GeloMyrtol in Europe).
safety: TOXIC if ingested undiluted - as little as 3.5 mL of pure oil can be fatal in children; keep away from children and never apply near an infant's face (can cause respiratory arrest). May lower blood sugar and interact with diabetes medications. Can paradoxically trigger asthma. Affects liver CYP enzymes with possible drug interactions. External use or controlled-dose capsules only.
origin: Aboriginal nations burned the leaves and inhaled the smoke for respiratory infection and used kino resin on wounds.

name: Lemon Myrtle
summary: Contains 90-98% citral, the highest natural concentration of any plant - higher than lemongrass - giving broad-spectrum antimicrobial, antifungal and antiviral activity documented against E. coli, Staphylococcus, Candida and Aspergillus in vitro. Very high antioxidant (ORAC) values and commercial use as a natural food preservative.
how: Dried leaf tea: steep 1 tsp 5-7 minutes for a pleasant lemon flavor. Use culinarily as a lemon substitute in cooking and baking. Diluted essential oil for topical antimicrobial use; also added to cleaning products.
safety: The essential oil is extremely high in citral and must be diluted for topical use or it causes skin sensitization and irritation; citral can cause contact dermatitis. Not for internal use as an essential oil. Leaves are safe as tea and food flavoring.
origin: Queensland rainforest leaves crushed by Aboriginal peoples for colds, sore throats, flavoring and insect repellence.

name: Kakadu Plum
summary: Holds the highest recorded natural vitamin C concentration of any plant - 1,000-5,300 mg per 100 g fresh weight, roughly 100x oranges - plus ellagic acid, gallic acid and lutein. Antimicrobial against Bacillus cereus, E. coli, Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, with antioxidant capacity among the highest of any food.
how: Freeze-dried powder 1/2 to 1 tsp daily in smoothies or food. Fresh fruit is seasonal in northern Australia. Also used in vitamin C skincare serums and extract supplements.
safety: Very high vitamin C means less is needed - overconsumption causes GI distress. May increase iron absorption, so caution in hemochromatosis. Limited safety data for concentrated supplements and oxalate content is not well characterized. Sustainability matters - source from Aboriginal-owned enterprises where possible.
origin: A wet-season fruit of Arnhem Land eaten for nutrition and used with the bark as an antiseptic for skin sores.

name: Bush Tomato
summary: Desert fruit rich in selenium (comparable to Brazil nuts), iron, vitamin C, zinc and potassium - about 5x a banana's potassium per gram - with citrulline, unusual carotenoids and documented antioxidant activity. High in dietary fiber and increasingly studied as a functional food ingredient.
how: Dried fruit rehydrated and added to stews, sauces and spice mixes, or ground as a seasoning. Bush tomato chutney is a popular Australian product, sold through bush food suppliers.
safety: Only Solanum centrale is safe - many wild Solanum species are toxic, so never forage without expert identification. Contains small amounts of solanine like other Solanums. Some people experience digestive discomfort.
origin: Dried on the bush and collected by Arrernte, Pitjantjatjara and Luritja peoples as a key desert survival food.

name: Wattle Seed
aka: Acacia victoriae, A. coriacea, A. aneura
summary: An extremely low glycemic index food (GI around 7) that is 26% protein and high in fiber, iron, zinc, magnesium, potassium and selenium, providing slowly digested carbohydrate with potential for diabetes management. Roasted wattleseed "coffee" is caffeine-free with a chocolate-hazelnut flavor.
how: Roasted and ground as a coffee substitute or added to baking, desserts and sauces; wattleseed flour for low-GI baking. Available from Australian bush food suppliers.
safety: Only certain Acacia species are edible and many are toxic - do NOT forage without expert guidance; use commercially sourced food-safe products. Some people are allergic to Acacia. Phytate content may reduce mineral absorption, mitigated by roasting.
origin: Ground into flour for bread across the continent - one of the oldest food-processing traditions on Earth.

name: Emu Oil
summary: Rendered fat about 40-50% oleic acid with omega-3, -6 and -9 fatty acids. Anti-inflammatory properties are documented in multiple animal studies (Whitehouse 1998, Inflammopharmacology), it penetrates skin deeply and enhances transdermal delivery, and wound-healing acceleration is shown in animal models, with pilot evidence for chemotherapy-related skin damage.
how: Apply pure emu oil topically to joints, muscles, wounds and dry skin; also used as a carrier oil. Sold in pharmacies and health stores, especially in Australia - look for refined, properly rendered oil from reputable sources.
safety: Not for internal consumption in quantity. Quality varies enormously with the rendering process and some products are adulterated with cheaper oils. May cause breakouts on acne-prone skin. Not suitable for vegans; emu farming raises ethical considerations.
origin: One of the most important animal-derived Aboriginal medicines, used for thousands of years on burns and joints.

name: Paperbark
summary: The papery bark provides a naturally sterile, breathable wound dressing, and the antimicrobial properties of Melaleuca species are well documented as relatives of tea tree, though formal clinical evidence for the bark specifically is lacking. Paperbark leaf oils contain terpenes similar to tea tree in different ratios.
how: Traditionally used as bandages for wounds and burns, food wrapping for cooking, baby wrapping, water vessels and shelter. Still used as a natural food wrapper that imparts subtle flavor; paperbark essential oils and extracts appear in Australian bush medicine products.
safety: Confirm species - some Melaleuca species are high in 1,8-cineole. Essential oils should not be ingested. Harvest sustainably, taking only outer layers. Consult Aboriginal communities regarding traditional use out of cultural respect.
origin: One of the most versatile plants in Aboriginal culture across northern and eastern Australia.

name: Native Pepperberry
aka: Tasmannia lanceolata, mountain pepper, Tasmanian pepper
summary: Contains polygodial, a potent antimicrobial, antifungal and anti-inflammatory sesquiterpene dialdehyde with strong activity against Candida via cell membrane disruption. Antioxidant activity is among the highest of any Australian food, and food-preservation effects against foodborne pathogens are confirmed.
how: Dried berries used sparingly as a pepper substitute - hot, peppery and slightly fruity with a fading heat; dried leaf used as a spice. Available in gourmet food stores and as an extract.
safety: Very potent - use sparingly, as it is hotter than black pepper. Polygodial can irritate mucous membranes at high doses and cause GI irritation if overconsumed. Allergic reactions possible; ensure correct species identification.
origin: Berries and leaves chewed by Tasmanian Aboriginal peoples for toothache and sore gums, and used to preserve food.

name: Davidson Plum
summary: A deep burgundy rainforest fruit very high in anthocyanins with very high measured antioxidant activity, plus potassium, vitamin E and lutein. Antimicrobial properties are documented and research interest as a functional food ingredient is growing, but medicinal use is minimally documented.
how: Used in jam, sauce and desserts, or as freeze-dried powder. Very tart, so it is typically eaten in processed or cooked forms. Available through Australian bush food suppliers.
safety: Very acidic - may irritate the stomach if eaten raw in quantity. The tree sap can cause skin irritation, hence the species name pruriens. Limited safety data for concentrated supplements.
origin: A Queensland rainforest food fruit; the bark was traditionally used as a fish poison for fishing.

name: Finger Lime
summary: A native Australian citrus rich in vitamin C, folate and potassium, containing the citrus flavonoids hesperidin and naringin with documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Its caviar-like vesicles carry the same beneficial compounds as other citrus in a unique texture, and citrus oil antimicrobial properties apply.
how: Cut open and squeeze out the citrus caviar pearls as a fresh garnish, or use in marmalade and preserves. Increasingly available in specialty food stores and commercially cultivated.
safety: Citrus allergy applies. Acidic - may exacerbate acid reflux. Generally very safe as a food.
origin: Eaten fresh for nutrition by rainforest Aboriginal peoples, with the juice applied to skin sores.

name: Quandong
aka: Santalum acuminatum, desert quandong, native peach
summary: Arid-zone fruit high in vitamin C, vitamin E, phenolics and rutin. The kernel contains unusual fatty acids including ximenynic and santalbic acid with documented anti-inflammatory properties, and extracts show antimicrobial and antioxidant activity; clinical data is very limited.
how: Dried fruit rehydrated for pies, sauces and desserts. Quandong kernel oil applied to skin as a moisturizing anti-inflammatory. Available through Australian bush food suppliers.
safety: The kernel shell is extremely hard and must be cracked to extract oil; seeds should not be eaten whole. Ensure correct species - some Santalum species are endangered. Limited safety data.
origin: A key arid-zone food; leaves and bark were poulticed for boils and rheumatism, and kernel oil used on skin and hair.

name: Gubinge (Billy Goat Plum)
summary: The same species as Kakadu plum under its Kimberley name, carrying the world's highest natural vitamin C concentration plus ellagic acid and exceptional antioxidant capacity, with documented antimicrobial activity against several bacterial pathogens.
how: As for Kakadu plum: freeze-dried powder 1/2 to 1 tsp daily in smoothies or food, fresh fruit in season, or extract supplements. Buying from Aboriginal-owned enterprises such as Kimberley Wild Gubinge ensures ethical sourcing and community benefit.
safety: Very high vitamin C - overconsumption causes GI distress and it may increase iron absorption, so caution in hemochromatosis. Limited safety data for concentrated supplements; oxalate content is not well characterized.
origin: Wild-harvested in the Kimberley wet season by Nyul Nyul and other peoples as a critical seasonal food and medicine.

name: Snake Vine
aka: Tinospora smilacina, related to T. cordifolia (guduchi)
summary: Contains berberine, palmatine and terpenoids with documented antimicrobial and preliminary anti-inflammatory activity. Its close relative Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi/giloy) is extensively studied for immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and hepatoprotective effects, but research on the Australian species specifically is thin.
how: Not widely commercially available; used mainly within traditional Aboriginal medicine contexts - vine crushed onto wounds and sores, inner juice squeezed and drunk for fever and pain. Follow traditional preparation under knowledgeable guidance.
safety: Limited safety data for T. smilacina specifically. NOT a proven snakebite treatment - seek emergency medical care for envenomation. May interact with immunosuppressant drugs if its immunomodulatory effects match T. cordifolia. May lower blood sugar. Do not self-identify the plant.
origin: An important medicinal vine of northern Australian Aboriginal pharmacopoeia, poulticed onto wounds and snakebites.
